claim: Early-life stress (ELS) paradigm combining limited bedding and nesting materials with maternal separation from postnatal days 10-17 induces lifelong stress susceptibility.
source: We employed an ELS paradigm which combines limited bedding and nesting materials as well as maternal separation from postnatal days 10–17 (Figure 1A) and has been shown to induce lifelong stress susceptibility (Peña et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Peña et al., 2017

claim: The ELS paradigm induces a latent increase in blood corticosterone with a significant increase occurring at P45, long after the termination of the stress paradigm.
source: Taking trunk blood from mice across several litters at different time points in the ELS paradigm – pre-stress (P10), end of ELS paradigm (P17), at the start (P45), and end of our experimental window (P70) – we report that this ELS paradigm induces a latent increase in blood corticosterone with a significant increase occurring only in late adolescence P45, long after the termination of the stress paradigm (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing corticosterone measurements at different time points, with Figure 1B showing the increase at P45

claim: ELS mice had increased time spent in closed arms of the elevated plus maze.
source: ELS mice had increased time spent in closed arms p=0.0276, naïve N = 18, ELS N = 11 mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the elevated plus maze task shown in Figure 1H

claim: ELS mice had decreased time spent in open arms of the elevated plus maze.
source: ELS mice had decreased time spent in open arms p=0.0276, naïve N = 18, ELS N = 11 mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the elevated plus maze task shown in Figure 1I

claim: Total distance travelled during elevated plus maze test was increased by ELS.
source: Total distance travelled during elevated plus maze test was increased by ELS. p=0.02, naïve N = 9, ELS N = 11 mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the elevated plus maze task shown in Figure 1J

claim: Total distance travelled during open-field test was increased in ELS mice.
source: Total distance travelled during open-field test was increased in ELS mice. p=0.04, naïve N = 9, ELS N = 14 mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the open-field task shown in Figure 1F

claim: Increased locomotion in response to stress is consistent with previous reports.
source: Increased locomotion in response to stress is consistent with previous reports (Füzesi et al., 2016; Sharma et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Auditory discriminative fear conditioning requires synaptic plasticity changes in the lateral amygdala.
source: We employed an auditory discriminative fear conditioning paradigm that requires synaptic plasticity changes in the lateral amygdala (Kim and Cho, 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kim and Cho, 2017

claim: ELS did not affect % freezing to neutral and aversive auditory cues during learning.
source: ELS did not affect % freezing to neutral and aversive auditory cues during learning. Naïve N = 20, ELS N = 17.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C

claim: During memory recall, ELS mice exhibited enhanced fear responses to neutral cues (CS-) with no difference in freezing to conditioned cues (CS+) compared to naïve mice.
source: In contrast, memory recall was affected with ELS mice exhibiting enhanced fear responses to neutral cues (CS-; Figure 2D, grey area), with no difference in freezing to conditioned cues (CS+; Figure 2D) compared to naïve mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D

claim: Discrimination Index was impaired by ELS.
source: Discrimination Index was impaired by ELS. p=0.004, naïve N = 20, ELS N = 17.

evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from slice electrophysiology shown in Figure 2G and H

claim: Fear acquisition in ELS mice resulted in a significant increase in c-Fos density, suggestive of increased excitability levels.

source: Genetic perturbation of amygdala astrocyte function by either reducing astrocyte calcium activity or reducing astrocyte network function was sufficient to replicate cellular, synaptic, and fear memory generalisation associated with early-life stress.

claim: The ELS paradigm overlaps with the stress hyporesponsive period, a time window during which stressors fail to elicit increases in blood corticosterone levels.
source: While the lack of endocrine response to stress during the stress paradigm might appear paradoxical, this ELS paradigm overlaps with the stress hyporesponsive period, a time window during which stressors fail to elicit increases in blood corticosterone levels (Schmidt et al., 2003; Sapolsky and Meaney, 1986; Schmidt, 2019; Vázquez, 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Similar to our findings, others have reported latent increases in blood corticosterone levels following ELS that were associated with increased anxiety-like behaviour and fear generalisation later in life.
source: Indeed, similar to our findings, others have reported latent increases in blood corticosterone levels following ELS that were associated with increased anxiety-like behaviour (Sharma et al., 2022) and fear generalisation (Elliott and Richardson, 2019) later in life.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Fear generalisation is a common trait observed in anxiety disorders.
source: The primary behavioural phenotype revealed by this work, that is, fear generalisation, is a common trait observed in anxiety disorders (Dymond et al., 2015; Lissek and van Meurs, 2015; Lis et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Astrocytes have been shown to directly regulate synaptic transmission and plasticity.
source: Glial cells, which comprise approximately half the cell population in the brain, have been shown to directly regulate synaptic transmission and plasticity (Murphy-Royal et al., 2015; Murphy-Royal et al., 2020; Lau et al., 2021; Henneberger et al., 2010; Papouin et al., 2017; Covelo and Araque, 2018; Panatier et al., 2011; Panatier et al., 2006; Matos et al., 2018; Lefton et al., 2024; Guttenplan et al., 2024)
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies

claim: Astrocytes influence many discrete behaviours.
source: thereby influencing many discrete behaviours (Nagai et al., 2021; Wahis et al., 2021; Robin et al., 2018; Martin-Fernandez et al., 2017; Yu et al., 2018; Nagai et al., 2019; Doron et al., 2022; Adamsky et al., 2018; Kol et al., 2020; Mu et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2024).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies

claim: Astrocytes have important roles in regulating affective states, fear, reward and addiction behaviours.
source: Despite research suggesting important roles for astrocytes in regulating affective states (Wahis et al., 2021; Martin-Fernandez et al., 2017), fear (Martin-Fernandez et al., 2017), reward and addiction behaviours (Doron et al., 2022; Kruyer et al., 2022; Kruyer et al., 2019)
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies

claim: The amygdala is involved with threat detection and associative learning that is acutely sensitive to stress.
source: This task was specifically chosen to test the effects of ELS on amygdala function as this brain region is involved with threat detection and associative learning that is acutely sensitive to stress (Guadagno et al., 2018b; Guadagno et al., 2021; Ressler, 2010; Malter Cohen et al., 2013; Roozendaal et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies

claim: The vast majority of studies report that astrocyte dysfunction impairs memory across various brain regions.
source: Astrocytes have long been shown to be critical for memory formation, with the vast majority of studies reporting that astrocyte dysfunction impairs memory across various brain regions (Robin et al., 2018; Yu et al., 2018; Depaauw-Holt et al., 2024; Sun et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies

claim: c-Fos levels inversely correlate with memory accuracy in hippocampal circuits.
source: In support of this notion, evidence of a cellular mechanism whereby c-Fos levels inversely correlate with memory accuracy has been recently shown in hippocampal circuits (Asok et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Asok et al., 2018

claim: Early-life experience strongly shapes episodic memory development, with stress delaying maturation of memory processes.
source: In addition, early-life experience strongly shapes episodic memory development, with stress delaying maturation of memory processes (Ramsaran et al., 2024).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ramsaran et al., 2024

claim: Early-life stress has been shown to activate specific neuronal ensembles that contribute to stress hypersensitivity.
source: Early-life stress has even been shown to activate specific neuronal ensembles that contribute to stress hypersensitivity (Balouek et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Balouek et al., 2023

claim: Astrocytes potentially form part of engram stabilisation or are directly recruited into engrams.
source: Further support comes from recent demonstration of astrocyte-engram neuron interactions with astrocytes potentially forming part of engram stabilisation or even direct recruitment of astrocytes into engrams (Williamson et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Williamson et al., 2024 and Kim et al., 2023

claim: Astrocytes participate in memory formation and consolidation.
source: Our data are in line with previous reports that have demonstrated clear roles for astrocytes in memory formation and consolidation (Martin-Fernandez et al., 2017; Adamsky et al., 2018; Kol et al., 2020)
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies

claim: The impact of CalEx on discrimination memory was more robust in female mice compared to males.
source: We found astrocyte calcium events were larger in amplitude and size in female mice compared to males. This higher basal activity could explain why CalEx induced a more profound impairment in fear discrimination in female mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and involves inference about the mechanism

Female ELS mice freeze significantly more to CS+ (right) than male counterparts, p<0.0001. Female N = 9, Male N = 8.

evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Williamson et al., 2024

source: As such, we quantified the percentage of astrocytes expressing the activity marker c-Fos following fear conditioning in mice and report similar values to those found in the hippocampus (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A and B) suggestive of modest recruitment of astrocytes in amygdala-dependent memory engrams.
